summary: Defines a NETCONF capability that adds partial lock and unlock operations. Standard NETCONF can only lock an entire configuration datastore, but sometimes only parts need to be locked. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Instead of locking the whole classroom while you fix one desk, this lets you put a lock on just that desk, so others can work on the rest.

questions: how to lock part of a netconf datastore
what is the netconf partial lock rpc
how does partial-lock work in netconf
can netconf lock only part of the running datastore
subtitle: Lock just the parts of a NETCONF running datastore you are editing, so other managers can keep working on the rest.

tldr.problem: The base NETCONF lock operation locks an entire configuration datastore, which stops other managers from working in parallel even when they touch unrelated parts.
tldr.mechanism: A new :partial-lock capability adds partial-lock and partial-unlock operations. The client picks nodes with XPath expressions, and the server locks those nodes and everything beneath them in the running datastore, all or nothing.
tldr.outcome: Several managers can edit different areas of the same device at once. The lock only guards writes, is released when the session ends, and is meant for consistency, not for access control.

today: RFC 5717 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the partial lock capability for NETCONF, and the RFC includes a non-normative YANG module alongside the normative XML schema.

sections.title: Why Lock Only Part of a Datastore
sections.content:
The base NETCONF protocol (RFC 4741) has lock and unlock operations that work on an entire configuration datastore. Often, though, several management sessions need to change the configuration of a managed device in parallel.

RFC 5717 defines a capability-based extension that locks only the running datastore, and only parts of it. The parts are chosen with the existing XPath filtering mechanism. The capability is identified by urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:partial-lock:1.0.
sections.eli5: Locking everything just because you want to change one thing makes everybody else wait. This lets you lock only the bit you are changing.

sections.title: Scope, Protected Area and Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC defines three terms. An Instance Identifier is an XPath expression naming one specific node, written as an absolute path in abbreviated syntax. The scope of the lock is the set of nodes returned by the XPath expressions when the lock is granted. The protected area is the scope plus all nodes in the subtrees beneath them.

Two usage scenarios are described. In the first, managers work on overlapping sections of the running datastore, so each locks what matters for the task, edits, and releases the lock quickly (seconds rather than minutes). In the second, the data model has well-separated areas, so each manager locks an assigned area and can hold it for minutes or hours without hindering anyone. That scenario assumes the global lock is not used.

The system MUST make sure that locked resources are not changed by other NETCONF operations or by non-NETCONF means such as SNMP and the command line interface.
sections.eli5: The locked desks are the scope. The desks plus everything inside them are the protected area. Nobody else can touch any of it until you are done.

sections.title: The partial-lock Operation
sections.content:
The client sends one or more select elements, each holding an XPath expression that MUST return a node set; at least one node set must be non-empty. Without the :xpath capability the expression MUST be an Instance Identifier. On success the reply carries a lock-id and a list of locked-node entries.

The XPath expressions are evaluated only once, at lock time. After that the scope is kept as a fixed set of nodes. A new interface created later is therefore not locked, even if the original expression would now match it. If the lock owner deletes a locked node, it leaves the scope; if all are deleted, the lock stays with an empty scope.

The operation is atomic: the server locks all requested parts or none, and unlocks anything already locked if one part fails. A session MAY hold several partial locks, and where they overlap the common area stays protected until all of them are released.

Locking protects against writes only. Reads are unaffected, and data outside the protected area can still be edited. The client must lock every part that matters to its change.
sections.eli5: You hand over a list of desks and get a ticket number. Either every desk on your list gets locked, or none do. The list is fixed at that moment.

sections.title: When a Lock Fails and How to Avoid Deadlock
sections.content:
A <partial-lock> MUST fail if any session, including the requester, holds the global lock on the running datastore; if any part is already locked by another management session, NETCONF or not; if the user is not authenticated; or if access control denies it.

The error tags are specific. An invalid XPath gives invalid-value; a non-node-set result adds not-a-node-set; all-empty results give operation-failed with no-matches; a non-Instance Identifier without :xpath gives invalid-lock-specification; and a conflict gives lock-denied with the session-id of the owner (0 for a non-NETCONF owner). Access control SHOULD be checked before conflicting locks, so an unauthorized client learns nothing about other sessions.

To avoid deadlock, clients SHOULD lock everything they need in one operation. If locking fails, the client MUST back off, release locks it already holds, and SHOULD retry after a randomized wait.
sections.eli5: If someone else already has your desk, you get told who. To avoid two people each holding one thing the other needs, ask for everything at once, and if it fails, put it all back and wait a random time.

sections.title: Unlocking and Effects on Other Operations
sections.content:
The <partial-unlock> operation takes a lock-id that the same session received earlier and has not already released. Only that lock is removed, even if locks overlap. An unknown or foreign id gives an invalid-value error. A positive reply is sent even if all the locked nodes have since been deleted.

While a partial lock is held, other sessions that try to modify the protected area get error tag in-use with app-tag locked. This covers edit-config, copy-config, delete-config, commit and discard-changes aimed at the running datastore. With continue-on-error, an edit-config may still change unprotected parts. The global lock fails if any partial lock exists, even one owned by the same session.
sections.eli5: Handing back your ticket number unlocks just that lock. Anyone else who tries to change your locked desk is told it is in use.

sections.title: Interaction With Other NETCONF Capabilities
sections.content:
Partial locking works only on the running datastore. The candidate datastore and the startup datastore cannot be locked with <partial-lock>.

If the server supports confirmed commit and a confirmed commit is still waiting for its confirming commit, the partial lock MUST be denied, because the server might have to roll the running datastore back. The error is in-use with app-tag outstanding-confirmed-commit.
sections.eli5: If the teacher might still undo recent changes, you cannot lock the desk yet, because the teacher may need to move things around.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same considerations apply as for base NETCONF. The operations MUST only be allowed for an authenticated user and SHOULD only be allowed for an authorized user, although NETCONF access control is not standardized and so this is strongly recommended but OPTIONAL.

A lock could be misused to keep others out, so the RFC lists safeguards: unauthenticated users never get a lock, a lock is released automatically when its session ends however it ends, and kill-session can terminate another session, which also frees a lock hung by a broken TCP connection. Servers MAY log lock requests in an audit trail.

Partial locking is not an authorization mechanism and SHOULD NOT be used for access control. It should only provide consistency among managers, and the scope is fixed at grant time so users can see exactly what is locked.
sections.eli5: A lock is a courtesy to keep people from bumping into each other, not a security guard. Only people who are logged in can use it, and an administrator can break a stuck lock.

sections.title: Example: Reserving a New Node
sections.content:
Partial lock cannot lock a node that does not exist yet. Appendix C shows how to reserve one: lock the parent, create the new node, lock that new node with a second partial-lock, then release the parent lock.

In the example a manager wants to add user Joe under users. Locking all existing user nodes would not cover Joe, so the whole users node is locked first (lock-id 1). Joe is created with edit-config, then a second lock covers only Joe (lock-id 2), and finally lock-id 1 is released so other managers can add users.
sections.eli5: To save a seat that is not there yet, you hold the whole row, put the new chair in, claim just that chair, and then let go of the row.
